items: Understand the Impulse Control Gap: Recognize that your toddler's hitting comes from a brain that isn't finished building impulse control yet, not from a character flaw or bad intentions.

Understand the Impulse Control Gap: Reframe your toddler's hitting as a timing problem rather than a behavior problem, understanding that their brain physically cannot do what you're asking of them yet.
Understand the Impulse Control Gap: Observe your child for early warning signs before hitting episodes occur, watching for hand flapping or other signals that indicate they are becoming dysregulated.
Understand the Impulse Control Gap: Identify which of the four root triggers—overstimulation, frustration, physical discomfort, or attention-seeking—typically drives your child's aggression.
Read Pre-Aggression Body Language: Watch your child for early warning signs like hand flapping, facial tension, or sudden withdrawal that signal aggression is building before it erupts.
Read Pre-Aggression Body Language: Intervene at the earliest sign of dysregulation rather than waiting for the hit to occur, moving closer and speaking softly to interrupt the pattern.
Read Pre-Aggression Body Language: Match your response to the specific trigger you identified, not applying the same generic solution to every situation your child faces.
Read Pre-Aggression Body Language: Practice calm, consistent redirection when you catch the signals, saying no firmly while offering a sensory break to prevent escalation.
Build Your Regulation Scaffolding: Function as your child's external regulation system by staying calm and providing predictable responses that their brain cannot yet generate internally.
Build Your Regulation Scaffolding: Check your expectations before reacting to your child's behavior, asking yourself what you are expecting them to do that their brain is not yet capable of.
Build Your Regulation Scaffolding: Create sensory support strategies such as finding a quiet space, reducing noise, or offering a comfort object when overstimulation triggers aggression.
Build Your Regulation Scaffolding: Maintain your own regulation by pausing and taking a breath before responding, understanding that your calmness directly influences their ability to regulate.
